title: The Bird Opening
description: Take flight with this amazing offbeat weapon. The Bird creates a central blockade with simple plans, often turning into huge attacks onto our opponent. Recommended for intermediate and advanced Chessly users.

2kr1b1r/1pp2ppp/p1nqp3/3p4/2PPnPb1/1Q2PN.text:
Castling does save it, but it gives us an idea.

We don't have to fight in the center anymore.

We can close it to our advantage.

We push and hit the queen.

This gives us tempo to continue with our operations.

Once we've closed the center like this, a good idea is to continue pushing.

2kr1b1r/1ppq1ppp/p1n1p3/2Pp4/3PnPb1/Q3PN.text:
First we have to side step to a3 in order to open up the b-pawn's path.

We will push and eventually try to attack on the queenside.

As you can see, the Bird can be very flexible in terms of attacking on either side.

You just have to know which setup to use when you anticipate Black castling queenside, like we did here with 5.d4.

2kr1bnr/1pp1p1pp/p1nq1p2/1B1p4/3P1Pb1/4P.text: If Black pushes ...a6 here, we have an interesting sacrifice.

2kr1bnr/1pp1p1pp/p1nq1p2/1B1p4/P2P1Pb1/4.text:
This is called the Fishing Pole.

We sacrifice the bishop in order to open up the a-file for the rook.

There is no merit to Black capturing on b5 as they will have to defend the whole game.

We would find compensation quickly.

2kr1bnr/p1p3pp/2p2p2/3p4/3P1P2/4P3/PPPN2.text:
And leave us the bishop.

In the end, we've managed to grab  a pawn and Black's c-pawns are doubled.

White is much better here.
So they basically have to capture the knight.

2kr1bnr/ppp1p1pp/2nq1p2/1B1p4/3P1Pb1/4PN.text:
Black goes for ...f6, which is a sensible move.

They want to control the e5-square and even push ...e5.

We have other plans as well.

We want to push c4 here and try to break through since Black has castled long.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2nq4/1B1p4/3P1Pb1/4PN2/.text:
And they might castle queenside right away.

We'll get our king into safety first.

That's always a priority.

2kr1bnr/ppp3pp/2Bq1p2/3pp3/3P1Pb1/4PN2/P.text:
Let's capture the knight first.

This will serve a purpose very soon, as you will see.

2kr1bnr/ppp3pp/2nq1p2/1B1pp3/3P1Pb1/4PN2.text:
Going for ...e5 is a mistake.

There is actually a tactic in here that wins us a pawn.

Let's capture the knight first.

This will serve a purpose very soon, as you will see.

2kr1bnr/ppp3pp/2q2p2/3pN3/3P1P2/4P3/PPPN.text:
They take the queen instead.

And we will take their queen, of course.

Now the rook is under attack.

2kr1bnr/ppp3pp/2q2p2/3pp3/3P1Pb1/4PN2/PP.text:
Black will most likely recapture with the queen to keep their pawn structure intact.

Do you see a tactic here?

It's to take on e5 with the knight!

We capture a pawn and attack Black's queen while hanging our own.

If Black takes the knight, we will capture the bishop with check.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/5P2/4PN2/P.text:
Activating the bishop to b5 is the way to go.

Black often wants to develop their light-squared bishop which this move restricts as they should defend with ...Bd7.

Otherwise, we are threatening to double Black's pawns.

4...Bg4 transposes to the main line.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
They can play the two knights system, developing the knight to f6.

It's played 22% of the time.

This position can sometimes transpose, but our initial response should stay the same.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
Meanwhile, Black is often going to develop in the most natural way when placing a pawn on d5.

The knight controls the d4-square. 2...Nc6 is played 24% of the time.

The pawn chain we create with e3 is a common theme in the Bird: our main idea is to control the central dark squares.

Our dark-squared bishop is blocked for the moment but we have a plan for it: b3 and Bb2!

On a side note, it is usually not good to play d4 when we're already played f4. This would leave the e4-square very weak, and our dark-squared bishop would have a hard time developing.

r2q1rk1/1pp1bppp/p1b1p3/3pP3/6Q1/1P1PPR2.text:
I suggest a rook lift here.

Our rook is coming to g3 to threaten the king, after which we will develop the knight and bring the a-rook to the game.

Black can't play ...Bf6 to defend and their position is cramped.

White is better.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1bbp3/3pP3/6Q1/1P1PP3/P.text:
We will recapture with the pawn.

This forces the bishop on d6 to move and gives us another tempo to continue our attack.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1bbp3/3pn3/5PQ1/1P1PP3/.text: Black has to trade here not to let our bishop come alive.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1bbpn2/3pN3/5P2/1P1PP3/.text: First, d3 is a solid move to open up a square for our b-knight.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1bbpn2/3pN3/5P2/1P2P3/P.text: If Black castles here, it's like giving you the green light to attack.

r2q1rk1/1ppn1ppp/p1bbp3/3pN3/5P2/1P1PP3/.text:
Black will most likely try to deal with our knight on e5.

But moving the knight away from f6 can prove to be dangerous for them.

r2q1rk1/1ppn1ppp/p1bbp3/3pN3/5PQ1/1P1PP3.text:
As it opens up the g4-square for our queen!

Suddenly, the bishop and the queen are eyeing the g7-pawn.

r2q1rk1/2p1bppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P1PPN2.text:
Black castles...

And we'll bring the knight to d2.

From there, the knight controls the key c4 and e4-squares and supports the knight on f3, which is especially helpful when Black plays ...Bg4.

r2q1rk1/2p1bppp/p3pn2/2pp4/5Pb1/1P1PPN2/.text:
Expect Black to push ...c5 at some point.

That's free space to be grabbed and Black wants to undouble their pawns at some point.

We don't have to worry about that now, however.

We can simply slide the queen to e1 and unpin.

Since we played f4, the queen often gets developed to the kingside from where it targets the light-squared bishop.

Also, the g3-square is a good square for the queen if you want to organize an attack, for example.

r2q1rk1/p1p1bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P1PPN2.text:
Well, the best plan is to push d3 here and open up a square for the knight.

Our knight on b1 will often move to d2 to support the other one.

At some point, you can also slide the queen to e1 and look to transfer it to the kingside.

r2q1rk1/p1p1bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/.text:
And so will Black.

How to continue now?

r2q1rk1/pppbbppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/5P2/1P1PPN.text:
And we will grab a bit more space with d3.

The idea is to often activate the knight to d2 and continue expansion with a move like Qe2.

At some point, we could even look to play e4.

r2qk1nr/1ppb1ppp/p3p3/3pP3/P5P1/1P2PQ2/1.text:
Extremely passive.

Black doesn't have a single active piece while our position is blossoming.

r2qk1nr/1ppb1ppp/p3p3/3pP3/P5PP/1P2PQ2/1.text:
When the g-pawn advances, you can continue with the h-pawn!

This type of pawn storm signifies an attack incoming.

It's extremely dangerous for Black to castle kingside.

r2qk2r/1p1bnppp/p3p2P/2ppP3/P5P1/1P2PQ2/.text:
But we will shove the pawn as far as h6 if allowed!

Black's lack of activity and defense has allowed us to challenge their g7-pawn.

They could get in a lot of trouble from here, if we continue with moves like Rf1 and transfer the knight to the kingside via c3 and e2.

White is much better.

r2qk2r/1p1bnppp/p3p3/2ppP2P/P5P1/1P2PQ2/.text: Black doesn't have many options but to advance in the center.

r2qk2r/1pp2ppp/p1bbpn2/3pN3/5P2/1P2P3/PB.text: Let's castle and keep our strong knight on e5.

If Black continues with ...Bd6, we don't even have to capture the bishop on c6.

We can continue in a positonal manner for now and soon look to transform the game into an attack.

r2qk2r/1ppb1ppp/p2bpn2/3pN3/P4P2/1P2PQ2/.text:
Black can try to activate their pieces, but won't get far.

We don't mind them capturing on e5.

r2qk2r/1ppb1ppp/p2bpn2/3pN3/P4PP1/1P2PQ2.text:
We'll just continue with g4, threatening g5.

Grabbing even more space on the kingside.

r2qk2r/1ppb1ppp/p3pn2/3pP3/P5P1/1P2PQ2/1.text: This forces one of Black's most important defenders to move, which is the knight on f6.

r2qk2r/1ppb1ppp/p3pn2/3pb3/P4PP1/1P2PQ2/.text: If Black captures, it is actually better to recapture with the pawn.

r2qk2r/1ppbnppp/p3p3/3pP2P/P5P1/1P2PQ2/1.text:
But we will shut that down by playing h5.

Now the g6-square is covered.

r2qk2r/1ppbnppp/p3p3/3pP3/P5PP/1P2PQ2/1B.text: They will probably try to develop the knight to e7, with the idea of bringing it to g6.

r2qk2r/2p1bppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black will prepare to castle too.

The next piece to develop is the b1-knight.

We don't want to activate it to c3 because it doesn't have much potential to jump to an active square from there.

d2 is a better square, so we'll prepare that development by playing d3.

r2qk2r/p1p1bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Once again, we have a straightforward plan. 

d3, Nd2 and Qe2 or Qe1 to h4.

Actually, we encounter this sequence of moves in multiple lines in this chapter.

That means it is important to remember the setups like this one.

We'll bring the king to safety.

Black activates the bishop to e7 now, and this is a standard position you might get many times in the Bird.

We will simply castle and look to play d3 and Nd2 next.

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
It's to just castle in this position.

The king is safe and we can continue development next.

Black activates their bishop as well, preparing to castle.

Let's show a calmer and more of a positional plan next.

r2qkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1b2n2/3p4/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop and keeps their pawn structure, but the bishop is only staring at the pawn on d5.

Besides, we will use our control of the e5-square soon and get the knight there to attack the bishop.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1b1pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text: Now it's logical for Black to continue with ...e6, opening up their bishop.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1b1pn2/3pN3/5P2/1P2P3/P.text:
But we will use the e5-square now.

Tehnically, this is the best move-order to threaten the bishop.

Otherwise, good players will play ...b6 and ...Bb7.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/1b1pN3/5P2/1P2P3/P.text: Black can try to preserve the bishop, but that only leads to us getting more free tempi and expanding while chasing it.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/1b1pN3/P4P2/1P2P3/.text: And we will do that with a4 here.

r2qkb1r/1ppb1ppp/p3pn2/3pN3/P4P2/1P2P3/1.text:
Once the bishop retreats, we don't have to capture it.

Our knight on e5 is stronger than that bishop.

We don't even have to play solidly; we can continue with an active approach that could eventually lead to an attack.

r2qkb1r/1ppb1ppp/p3pn2/3pN3/P4P2/1P2PQ2/.text:
And that is because Black's setup is passive.

We want to play g4 and g5 now.

Our king is actually safe on e1 since we have a lot of space.

r2qkb1r/2p1pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black will play ...Nf6 at some point.

And we'll fianchetto.

r2qkb1r/2p2ppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PQ2/PB.text:
We simply recapture with the queen.

The capture on f3 can happen any time, but it's not something likely to cause us problems.

r2qkb1r/2p2ppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P.text:
The standard setup for Black as well.

These past few moves illustrate the most important approaches for both sides which are seen in a lot of variations in this study.

We'll castle, having developed almost all the minor pieces.

r2qkb1r/p1p1pppp/2p2n2/3p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPP.text:
And worsen their pawn structure.

After that, we can continue with our usual plan of developing the dark-squared bishop.

Black doesn't really have any threats on our knight.

r2qkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P.text:
The best they can do right now is to open up their own bishop.

We'll fianchetto ours.

Black will continue natural development...

And we will complete the fianchetto.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/5Pb1/4PN2/P.text:
Black can ignore our threat and simply develop.

In which case we will capture...

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/5P2/1P2PN2.text:
Black can also choose to play ...e6, which completely blocks their light-squared bishop.

In this case, one of the plans is to continue natural development.

The other one is aggressive.
We'll get the bishop out to b2.

The aggressive plan we could go for abstains from castling.

Instead, we could try to get an attack going with Qe2 and Rg1 to build up for g4.

The additional kingside space with the pawn already on f4 is one of the biggest benefits of the Bird.

r2qkb1r/pppbpppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
We don't have to rush with capturing the knight.

Let's just prepare for the bishop to develop and wait for ...a6.

r2qkb1r/pppbpppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/5P2/4PN2/PP.text:
The most common move is to block the attack with the bishop.

It does look passive, but Black shouldn't split their pawn structure.

r2qkbnr/1pp1pppp/p1n5/1B1p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PP.text:
Black attacking the bishop only helps our cause.

We wanted to capture anyway.

r2qkbnr/2p1pppp/p1p5/3p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
Black recaptures, and here comes the standard plan to develop the dark-squared bishop.

We will use this setup in many lines of the Bird.

The bishop proves to be very active on the long diagonal.

And we keep the flexibility of pushing the d-pawn without having to worry about developing the bishop.

r2qkbnr/p1p2ppp/2p1p3/3p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP.text:
Once Black recaptures, it's time to develop our dark-squared bishop.

And the best plan is b3 and Bb2, as per usual.

r2qkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
The most common approach is the more active one, with Black choosing to pin our knight.

The idea is to develop the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6.

You will face this move 31% of the time.

I suggest the active Bb5 here.

Instead of defending passively with Be2, we pin Black's knight and threaten to capture it, doubling the black pawns.

r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/1B1p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PP.text:
Black opening up the dark-squared bishop here doesn't change much in our plan.

We'll still capture on c6.

r3kb1r/1pp1pppp/p1nq1n2/3p4/3P1Pb1/4PN2/.text:
Black does have a countermeasure, however.

And that is to place the knight on the e4-square, which is the downside of playing d4.

We'll castle.

There's not much we can do to stop the knight.

r3kb1r/1pp1pppp/p1nq4/3p4/3PnPb1/4PN2/PP.text:
However, once Black does go for ...Ne4, we should implement one of our main ideas in this variation and go after the defender of the knight.

This move also helps grab central space and potentially attack on the queenside.

And that's to expand with c4.

r3kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1nqp3/3p4/2PPnPb1/4PN2/P.text:
You will most likely face Black defending with ...e6.

But once we play c4, we should continue playing the queenside.

That is where Black will most likely castle soon.

Can you see a way to threaten something on the queenside?

Firstly, let's activate the queen and target the b7-pawn.

r3kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1nqpn2/3p4/3P1Pb1/4PN2/P.text: If they continue rather passively, we can just improve.

We support the knight and prepare Ne5.

After that, the c4-advance will be a natural follow-up.

r3kbnr/1pp1pppp/p1nq4/1B1p4/3P1Pb1/4PN2/.text:
If Black pushes ...a6 here, we won't capture, but rather move according to our plan.

And that's to retreat and unpin the knight.

Now there's a possibility of Ne5.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2nq4/1B1p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPP.text:
A move to consider is definitely ...Qd6.

We can't damage Black's structure here, so I propose a different plan.

It usually isn't advisable to push both d4 and f4 in the Bird, but specific lines require specific countermeasures.

One of the ideas is to bring the bishop back to e2 and then solidify the knight on the e5-square.

Another one is to push c4 and contest the center, sometimes even pushing c5 if Black castles queenside.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black's most popular first move is
1...d5, and it is played 36% of the time.

In the database, this is in more than 17 million games!

The logic is: if Black can't place their e-pawn in the center, they can take control of it with the d-pawn.

2.Nf3 is next.

We will have two pieces controlling e5. This is a common idea in our opening setups.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to The Bird course. 

In the first chapter, we will examine some of the most common positions you will encounter when playing this opening.

We will take a look at Black using different setups containing 1...d5, the most frequent response to our opening move of 1.f4.

In a rather unorthodox way of playing, we don't place a pawn on e4 or d4 on move 1.

However, we take control of the e5-square and plan to develop the knight to f3 without blocking the f-pawn.

2rqk2r/1p2bppp/p1b1pn2/2ppN3/5P2/1P1PP3/.text: And once Black gets the bishop out...

We'll do just that.

We've got an equal position on our hands.

Black will castle and maybe look to play ...b5, which is why a4 could be  a good idea.

We could capture the bishop on c6 at some point as well.

2rqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1b1pn2/2ppN3/5P2/1P2P3/P.text:
Black defends with ...Rc8.

The only minor piece left to activate is the knight on b1.

Developing it to c3 would block our bishop and from there the knight wouldn't have many active squares to jump to.

That's why I recommend d3 to develop it to d2.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pp4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
By far the most common third move is ...Nc6.

It's played 74% of the time.

Black activates the knight behind the pawn and grabs control of the center.

We would like to restrict their development. A good move to do that is Bb5, pinning the knight.

If Black doesn't protect it, we could capture and ruin their pawn structure.

r2q1rk1/p3bppp/2p1pn2/2pp4/5Pb1/1P1PPN2/.text:
And now our f3-knight is supported by another one.

White is slightly better here for the simple reason of leading in activity and having a better pawn structure.

All in all, a positional but comfortable game for White.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/5np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/PB.text: But what should our plan be after Black castles?

We'll develop the queen to e2.

Our expansion could consist of c4 and Nc3 to contest the center and block the c-file, especially if Black plays ...Rc8.

r2qk2r/p3bppp/2p1pn2/2pp4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/PB.text:
They get the bishop out.

As in the main line, developing the knight to c3 might be suboptimal, so we'll aim to get it out to d2.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/4pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
And the position is equal.

We are about to castle.

r2qk2r/pp1nppbp/5np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
And both bishops will find themselves on the long diagonal.

This structure for Black is rock solid.

We'll castle first.

r2qkb1r/1p2pppp/p1b2n2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
Standard moves by both sides in this line.

We'll complete the fianchetto.

We've got a lot of control of the central dark-squares, especially the e5-square.

This means that our knight is coming there.

r2qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1b1pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
Once Black plays ...e6, we can implement this idea.

Now we are attacking the bishop and threatening to disrupt Black's queenside structure again.

r2qkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PQ1P/P.text:
And now we can simply continue with b3.

The bishop is coming to b2, the knight is getting developed and we will castle.

There is nothing to worry about in this position.

r2qkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/5P2/4PQ1P/PPP.text: This is a small positional victory for us.

r2qkb1r/p3pppp/2p2n2/2pp4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/P1.text:
Expect Black to develop naturally as well.

The trade-off Black made is pinning our knight for the price of doubling their pawns.

We'll fianchetto now.

We still want to control those dark squares in the center even if Ne5 is currently impossible.

r2qkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/2pp4/5Pb1/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Black advances the e-pawn and opens up the dark-squared bishop.

We'll castle and expect Black to do so as well soon.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P1.text:
Since the light-squared bishop has been traded, Black can comfortably play ...e6.

Both sides will develop naturally.

r2qkb1r/pp1npp1p/5np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P1.text:
Setups with ...g6 are annoying because they are harder to attack.

But they are rare.

We'll develop the bishop to the optimal square...

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/2pp4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
The knight recaptures, and we can continue with standard development here.

The bishop can develop to b2, as per usual.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/5P2/4PQ1P/PPP.text:
Going for ...Nc6 now changes stuff up a bit.

I recommend we pin the knight.

The point is that Black has already traded their light-squared bishop so there is no ...Bd7.

This means that we will most likely be able to damage their structure.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/5P2/4PQ1P/P.text:
If Black continues with ...e6, just capture that knight.

And now Black has to damage their pawns.

r2qkbnr/1p1bpppp/p1n5/1Bpp4/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
Once Black attacks our bishop...

It's okay to capture.

Retreating would only give Black more momentum.

Besides, we basically placed the bishop on b5 to capture and remove Black's active knight.

r2qkbnr/1p2pppp/p1b5/2pp4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
Black will recapture with the bishop.

Let's continue with the standard developing plan for the dark-squared bishop.

We'll fianchetto.

r2qkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/2pp4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP2P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

We don't have to do anything with our knight yet, as Black doesn't have many threats.

The usual setup will suffice here, so let's fianchetto.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2n5/1Bpp4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP.text:
That's why ...Bd7 is sensible.

We'll just continue as per usual.

We'll castle, since we've developed the kingside fully.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1Bpp4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP.text:
Another idea Black could try is ...Bg4, counter-pinning our knight.

As mentioned, if Black doesn't protect the c6-knight, we should capture it.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/1Bpp4/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
Black blocks.

But a trade is okay here, as we don't want Black to have an active light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/5P2/4Pb1P/PPPP.text:
Black captures on f3, as there isn't much merit to retreating now.

Of course, ...Bh5 would get the bishop trapped.

And we will recapture with the queen.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/5Pb1/4PN2/PPPP.text:
Instead of going for ...Nc6 or ...c5, Black can continue with ...Bg4.

The idea is that Black wants to get the bishop out before playing ...e6.

We should deal with this pin as quickly as possible.

If we don't, ...c5 could arrive quickly, so we will attack the bishop right away.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PQ1P/P1.text: For example, b3, Bb2, and so on.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/4PQ1P/PPPP.text:
Black solidifies the center on the light squares, and the position is equal.

Natural development to follow.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
Black could activate the knight now, although they only do so 7% of the time.

It is a mix of the two main branches of this study.

I recommend a specific approach against this.

Let's develop with tempo. Be2 is too passive as an alternative.

All in all, I think b5 is the best square for our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
The move 2...Nf6 is played 17% of the time.

It sometimes transposes into positions we cover in other lines, but there are some specific setups we need to look at.

We will continue naturally with e3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1PP.text:
Apart from the Main Line, the move 2...c5 is the most popular move online.

It's played 18% of the time, in more than 2 million games!

We've given Black space and time to grab more central control, which is exactly why a lot of players play like this.

We'll continue as we usually do, creating a dark-square pawn chain.

The positions where e3 is a bad move in the Bird are rare.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black places a pawn in the center.

We'll develop our knight, pointing at e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Study 2, we will teach you how to play against setups that abstain from the 2...Nc6 Main Line.

In particular, we will show what to do when Black strikes in the center early with ...c5, or when they simply develop the kingside knight first.

We will open with the Bird.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1p1p/4p1p1/2ppP1b1/2P5/1P1BP.text:
We can play c4 for now.

White is slightly better with an active position.

Black shouldn't capture on e5 because of the Qg3 pin.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1p1p/4p1p1/2ppP1b1/8/1P1BP2Q.text:
Now the queen comes to c7 to attack our e5-pawn.

We don't have to protect it just yet, though.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1p1p/4p1pQ/2ppP1b1/8/1P1BP3.text:
The correct move is ...Bg5.

Black improves the bishop and targets our queen.

We will escape to h3, the only remaining square.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbp1p/4p1p1/2ppP2Q/8/1P1BP3/.text:
Blocking the threat with the g-pawn could work, but Black has to know what they are doing.

We will keep the queen close to the opponent's king.

Again, Black can't just make a move they think is good here.

There is a specific line where the position remains equal.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpp1/4p2p/2ppP2Q/8/1P1BP3/P.text: For example, the move ...h6 already gives us a huge advantage.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpp1/4p2p/2ppP2Q/8/1P1BPR2/.text:
We'll implement a rook lift, ready to slide to g3 and threaten the king even more.

If we need to, we will quickly play Na3 and bring the a-rook to the party.

White is much better.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4p3/2ppP3/8/1P1BP3/PBP.text:
Because if it is not on f6...

It's not defending the h7-pawn anymore!

The position is still equal, but Black has to be extremely precise when defending here.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P1BPN2.text:
And Black does so too.

It's time to start improving our pieces and opening up the queen.

The knight on f6 is Black's most important defender right now.

By centralizing our knight, we offer a trade.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2ppn3/5P2/1P1BP3/P.text:
Black removes our active knight, but for a price.

We will actually recapture with the pawn.

The main idea is to kick the knight away from f6.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P1BPN2/.text:
Black continues in a standard manner, simply developing.

This is usually good when you're playing a solid approach, but we've already got some angry bishops out.

If Black castles carelessly, we'll go for an attack.

First, we'll castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black continues with their plan, and here is an interesting developing move.

I suggest activating the bishop to d3!

It looks counter-intuitive because it blocks the d-pawn, but the bishop will prove to serve the best purpose on this square.

From there, it's eyeing the h7-square and is ready to help the attack as soon as possible.

r1bqr1k1/pp1nbp1p/4p1pQ/2ppP3/8/1P1BP3/P.text:
For example, sliding the rook to e8 loses on the spot.

Black mustn't leave the f7-pawn.

Because we will sacrifice the rook immediately!

r1bqr3/pp1nbk1p/4p1pQ/2ppP3/8/1P1BP3/PBP.text:
Black has to capture.

This leaves the h7-pawn hanging with check.

r1bqrk2/pp1nb2Q/4p1B1/2ppP3/8/1P2P3/PBPP.text:
It is the simple Bxg6, proving the strength of the light-squared bishop.

Now we are threatening two different checkmates in one and Black can't defend against both.

Good game.

r1bqrk2/pp1nb2Q/4p1p1/2ppP3/8/1P1BP3/PBP.text: Once the king moves, do you see the finisher?

r2q1rk1/pb1nbppp/1p2p3/2p1N1P1/4pP2/1P2P.text: As our knight it good, don't accept this trade if Black offers it.

r2q1rk1/pb1nbppp/1p2p3/2p3P1/4pPN1/1P2P3.text:
The knight is now very strong on g4, but our most important piece is the bishop on b2.

If we get the queen to the attack, this could get extremely dangerous for Black.

For example, if Black plays a random move like ...a6, Nh6+ is already crushing.

Black can't capture because of gxh6+, and moving the king to h8 runs into Qh5 in that case.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/1p2p3/2p3P1/4pP2/1P2PN2.text:
Black recaptures...

And we centralize our knight on e5.

Our plan is to rotate to g4 from where the knight targets the critical dark squares.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/1p2p3/2pp2P1/4nP2/1P1BP.text:
When faced with an attack on a side of the board, a general principle is to counter in the center.

But here the center is closed, so we have time to pursue our concept further.

As the knight on e4 is annoying and it is blocking our bishop, we will start by exchanging it off.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p2p3/3p4/4nPP1/1P1BPN.text:
Anticipating g5, many players will jump into the center here.

Black does have a clamp on the e4-square after all.

We will still push.

We don't have an immediate attack, but we managed to grab a lot of space.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p2pn2/3p4/5P2/1P1BPN2.text:
If Black just continues developing, they will have to endure some aggression.

And here it comes, with g4!

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bppp/1p2pn2/3p4/5P2/1P1BPN2.text:
As mentioned, Black will most likely go for a fianchetto approach as well.

And this is the moment where we can choose to be creative even without Black pushing ...c5.

We can try to force an attack with Rg1!

Although it comes with the cost of losing some castling rights, our idea is simple: g4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Once Black castles, we will go for the same developing move as in the main line.

We don't really need to push the d-pawn, so blocking it is actually not a problem here.

Our bishops stand strong.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PN2/P1P.text:
You will face 4...Be7 almost as often as 4...c5 here, as it is played 28% of the time.

Black just wants a solid setup with active pieces and no real fireworks on the board.

But we will still create them.

We will fianchetto first.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/P1P.text:
The move c5 is the most popular move in this position, played 30% of the time.

Black wants to grab space before activating the knight to c6 behind the pawn.

This is an active but a risky setup, where Black can easily become vulnerable to kingside attacks.

Let's activate the dark-squared bishop first.

It's incredibly strong on b2 already.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
And once Black continues by developing the knight...

We'll go for the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black responds with ...d5.

The standard second move, developing the knight behind the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1P.text:
Now Black creates a pawn chain in the center.

2...e6 is played 12% of the time, which is still in more than 1.3 million games.

This is a solid approach where Black wants to keep their pawns on the light squares and most often try to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

We'll open up our light-squared bishop and plan to fianchetto the other bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Study 3 will focus on the 1...d5 and 2...e6 approach by Black.

It is characterized by Black creating a light-squared pawn structure in the center and either trying to strike in the center, or maneuver around the structure and develop.

Let's open with the Bird.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1P2/2NBPN2.text:
Black finally castles...

And so will we.

Next, we will look to develop the dark-squared bishop to d2, but here it mainly depends on what Black will do.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/3p4/3P1P2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black can activate the knight, but it doesn't have any concrete threats.

We can continue developing ourselves.

It's up to Black to decide whether they want to protect the center with ...e6 and block the bishop or not.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1P2/2N1PN2/.text:
For now, they activate the knight and prepare castling.

We should place our bishop on the best square, too.

And that's d3.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1P2/2NBPb1P.text:
So they capture.

We will simply take back with the queen.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1Pb1/2NBPN2.text:
They decide to activate the bishop first and pin our knight.

Sure, this is fine, but the bishop will most likely have to trade.

Because when we attack it, there isn't really a good retreating square for Black.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1P2/2NBPQ1P.text:
We can play g4 to expand on the kingside, and continue with rook lifts like Rf2 to get better positioned for the attack. 

We can also choose to play on the queenside with a Rfb1/b4/a4 plan. 

Ideally, we choose one of the expansions and roll with it.
Now Black can play on the light squares, but we've got a lot of potential left in our position.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/8/3bPP2/2N1BQ2/P.text:
Black captures...

And we can pin the bishop here by castling.

This forces the bishops off, after which there are weaknesses around the black king and no pieces to defend them.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/8/4PP2/2N1bQ2/PP.text:
Black can capture with check.

Naturally we'll recapture on e3.

We've managed to get a couple of pieces out in no time and castled.

And Black's queen is under attack as well.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/3PPP2/2N1Bb2/P.text:
And they are.

They claim that we have to recapture with the pawn in order to save d4.

But our idea is to take back with the queen and offer the pawn!

We will receive a lot of compensation for the pawn.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/3PPPb1/2N2N2/P.text:
This pin is not that big of a deal anyway.

Because we have a defense and we've calculated what happens if Black is persistent. We'll support the d4-pawn with the bishop.

rn2qrk1/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/8/4PP2/2N1Q3/PP4P.text:
This means that we can use this momentum to attack on the kingside quickly, while Black's pieces are tangled up and passive.

And we will do so with h4!

Of course, h5 is the idea.

rn2qrk1/ppp1pp2/1n4p1/7p/4PP1P/2N1Q3/PP4.text:
Which is why Black blocks.

However, this is a big mistake.

Our attack is nowhere near over.

rn2qrk1/ppp1pp2/1n4p1/7p/4PPPP/2N1Q3/PP6.text:
The g4-pawn comes in as well!

If Black captures, h5 is coming.

If we manage to bust open the kingside, our pieces will be able to join the attack rapidly and we should already be winning.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/3PPP2/5N2/PP4P.text:
The knight retreats to b6 to keep the bishop open and attacking the pawn.

Black wants ...Bg4 now to pin our knight.

Nevertheless, we'll continue to develop towards the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3n4/3P1P2/4PN2/PP4.text:
Black castles.

Why shouldn't we grab space and attack their knight in the center?

All of our pawns on dark squares are defended.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3p4/2P2P2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black can react naturally and simply defend the pawn in the center. 

This is in fact the most popular move, happening in more than 2,500 games.

We'll capture once.

I prefer this to the immediate d4 because it opens up our bishop if we need it.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/6p1/3p4/5P2/4PN2/PP1P2P.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn.

And now it's time to contest the center.

With d4!

Black's bishop is neutralized and we have a huge clamp on the e5-square.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p4/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
Black fianchettoes. 

Black now contests the central dark squares more.

And we'll attack with the c4-pawn! 

4...dxc4 develops our bishop for us.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2P2P2/4PN2/PP1.text:
This defense is inferior for Black because it allows us to trade a flank pawn for a central one.

We will of course take them up on this offer.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3n4/5P2/4PN2/PP1P2P.text:
Black takes on d5. 

5...Qxd5 did not make sense because we would get in Nc3.

Now our center looks even more powerful after d4.

And when there isn't a pawn on d5, you should even aim for e4!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
And now this move, played in more than 200,000 games (around 2% of the total games), is a very important setup. 

Black has a dual strategy of the light squares with their d-pawn, and the dark squares with their g7-fianchetto.

To start countering, we will be consistent with our plan on the dark squares. 

We will later use our c-pawn to counter Black's central pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black goes for 1...d5, the most popular response.

We'll reinforce our control of the central e5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, I want us to explore Black doing for a d5 and g6 setup.

Black's d-pawn controls the central e4 light square, whereas the bishop exerts some control over the dark squares. 

It's necessary to come up with a strategy against this.

We'll begin with The Bird.

2k1r2r/ppp1qp2/2nb2p1/5b2/3PP1p1/2PQB1P1.text:
We will simply defend e4 and get out of the way on the next move.

Black can't add any more attackers to the pawn and White is much better once we castle queenside.

We are up a pawn and Black's g-pawns are doubled.

A natural move for Black here is ...Rde8, increasing the aggression on the pawn.

But it doesn't accomplish much other than preventing us taking the bishop on f5.

2kr2nr/pppq1p1p/2nbb3/8/6pN/2NP2P1/PPP1P.text:
And so do we.

Now we've also got the semi-open f-file for our rook.

Again, Black has nothing to show for the pawn and White is much better, with prospects of e4 or Ne4.

Black's own g-pawn is blocking the bishop and the queen.

2kr3r/ppp1qp2/2nb2p1/5b2/3PP1p1/2PQ2P1/P.text:
Black castles queenside now.

The king is safer and their rook can join the game.

On the other hand, we will get the bishop to e3.

Not only does this reinforce the center, but it also unpins the e4-pawn!

We are now threatening to capture the bishop on f5.

2kr3r/pppbq3/2nb2p1/5p2/3PP1p1/2PQB1P1/P.text:
But we don't have to capture and expose the e-file.

We can just strengthen the center instead and look to get the king to a safer square next and connect the rooks.

White is better.
Sure, Black can still try to strike in the center...

2kr3r/pppbqp2/2nb2p1/8/3PP1p1/2PQB1P1/PP.text:
The best move according to the computer is to simply retreat with the bishop.

Black keeps some chances here although White is still better.

The threat is now ...Rxh2.

We'll move away from the tactic by playing Kd1.

2kr4/ppp1qp2/2n3p1/5P2/3P2p1/2PQB3/PP4Bb.text:
We can take their bishop!

We are up a piece and completely winning.

2kr4/ppp1qp2/2n3p1/5b2/3PP1p1/2PQB1b1/PP.text:
The point is to win back the rook with this fork.

But we'll just move the king out of check.

2kr4/ppp1qp2/2nb2p1/5b2/3PP1p1/2PQB1P1/P.text:
Black might think they have a tactic here with ...Rxh2.

We'll take the rook.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2p1p/2nb4/8/6pN/6P1/PPPPP2P/.text:
Black could choose a less confrontational approach here and activate the knight, still claiming an advantage in activity.

That gives us time to consolidate, starting with d3.

Here we can implement a standard developing setup with the knight on c3 and the bishop on g2.

Don't make a mistake and play b3 here because there is ...Be5 and the position suddenly gets complicated!

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/2nb2p1/8/3P2p1/3Q2P1/PPP1.text:
Black continues with ...Nc6.

We don't want Black complicating matters with ...Nb4 or sacrificing the knight on d4.

So the move c3 covers both threats.

Still, Black can initiate some aggression in this line.

r2qk1nr/ppp2p1p/2nbb3/8/6pN/3P2P1/PPP1P2.text:
Black continues by getting the bishop out.

They will castle long since the kingside is weakened.

They have a lead in development now, but that won't prove to be decisive.

Especially when we get a knight that controls the center.

r2qk2r/ppp2p2/2nb2p1/5b2/3P2p1/2PQ2P1/PP.text:
And they definitely will use the chance to develop and attack your queen here.

If they know their theory you need to be prepared to defend a bit here.

The best defense is e4, blocking the attack and grabbing more central space.

r3k1nr/pppq1p1p/2nbb3/8/6pN/2NP2P1/PPP1P.text:
And, once Black prepares to castle long...

We also get a monster bishop on g2, eyeing that queenside.

We've consolidated and can only go up from here.

r3k2r/ppp1qp2/2nb2p1/5b2/3PP1p1/2PQ2P1/P.text:
They can pin the pawn, and we have to defend it again.

But we have a simple way of doing so.

And that's to place the bishop on g2.

Everything is defended so far.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qp2/8/7p/3P2p1/6B1/PPPQP2P/.text:
And now we simply bring the queen up one square. Once we get the knight out, we will be ready to castle queenside.

Our bishop on g3 is already extremely strong and will be joined by the other bishop on g2.

Meanwhile, Black hasn't achieved anything on the kingside other than over-extending. They are passive and their king is weak.

If Black goes for ...h4, don't be afraid to slide right back to f4.

The evaluation of this position is +2 for White.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2p2/8/7p/3P1Bpq/8/PPP1P2P/RN.text:
The queen comes in with check, but we played Bf4 for a reason.

And that's to block this check and grab a tempo.

rnbqk1n1/ppp1bp2/8/8/5Np1/6P1/PPPPP3/RNB.text:
And we take back.

The only thing left to do to prove our advantage is expand in the center, develop the queenside and then castle.

Black doesn't have anything here.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp1p/8/8/6pN/6P1/PPPPP2P/RN.text:
We could face ...Be7 immediately.

Black does move the bishop twice in the opening, but attacks our vulnerable knight.

We don't have time for Bf4.

So we will retreat to g2.

From there, the knight can jump to f4 and free up the g2-square for the bishop.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp2/8/7p/3P2pN/6P1/PPP1P2P/.text:
If Black lines up the bishop with the queen, claiming we don't have a lot of squares for the knight...

We can actually give the pawn back.

In the upcoming line, we will get a lot of activity and be clearly better.

One of the reasons we played d4 is so that we can play Bf4 here.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp2/8/7p/6p1/6P1/PPPPP1NP/R.text:
Especially when Black plays ...h5, with the intention of ...h4.

Now the knight is more active and still controlling some key squares.

Here, we have to be ready for ...h4.

Our goal is still to develop, but remain conscious of what Black is doing.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp2/8/8/5Np1/6Pp/PPPPP1BP/R.text:
What if Black pushes ...h3?

Well, they've just blocked all their fronts of attack on the kingside for a one-move threat on the bishop.

Although they do get some space.

We'll just move to the center.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp2/8/8/5Np1/6p1/PPPPP1BP/R.text:
Black can trade now, but that doesn't bother us anymore.

We'll simply recapture, and now the trade of rooks is basically inevitable.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp2/8/8/5Npp/6P1/PPPPP2P/RN.text:
And they will push that pawn.

Of course, we can't let them capture now that our h-pawn is pinned to the rook.

So we will play Bg2 and protect the rook while activating the bishop.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2p1p/3b4/6p1/8/5N2/PPPPP1PP/.text:
The move ...g5 is actually the most common move in this position, played 38% of the time!

Black is going all out on the early attack.

The obvious plan is ...g4, with Qh4+ to follow when the f3-knight moves.

To neutralize this, I recommend g3, blocking the potential queen check.

It's a good reaction to Black's last move without weakening our king too much.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2p1p/3b4/8/6p1/5NP1/PPPPP2P/.text:
You will face this push 70% of the time.

Black forces the issue, trying to make something out of the position.

I suggest we jump to h4.

We might need the knight on the kingside and from h4 we can move to g2 if needed.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2p2/3b4/6pp/8/5NP1/PPPPP2P/R.text:
Black doesn't have to play ...g4 first.

Around 20% of the time, players choose to follow up the g-pawn with the h-pawn.

This is obviously over-extending, but those pawns do look dangerous.

However, one of the best antidotes to the attack on a side of the board is playing in the center.

We'll expand, grabbing space and targeting the g-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2p2/3b4/7p/3P2p1/5NP1/PPP1P2.text:
The g5-pawn will most likely get pushed.

The knight is on the edge of the board but safe, and even restricting Black's light-squared bishop for now.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3b4/8/8/8/PPPPP1PP/RNBQ.text:
The bishop recaptures.

But what happens when we just continue natural development with Nf3?

We won't be that behind in development at all if the game continues peacefully, and Black won't have much to show for the pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bp2/5n2/8/4BNp1/2N3Pp/PPPPP2.text:
We'll develop and protect the bishop.

This trade is fine for us because despite potentially losing the bishop on the long diagonal, we will have two active knights and Black's lead in activity will diminish.
 
Remember that we are still up a pawn and Black has no attack. 

We'll castle kingside and maintain advantage.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bp2/5n2/8/4BNp1/6Pp/PPPPP2P/.text: Black can attack the bishop again, but we won't let them win more tempi.

rnbqk2r/ppp1np1p/3b4/8/6pN/6P1/PPPPP2P/R.text:
One of Black's ideas could be to rotate the knight to g6 and try to trade in order to open up the h-file.

This plan does work because our knight on h4 is restricted, but even if the h-file opens up we're fine.

We've got time to expand in the center with d4 and open up the dark-squared bishop.

We're also going to put the queen on d3. You'll see why.

rnbqk2r/ppp2p1p/3b2n1/8/3P2pN/6P1/PPP1P2.text:
Black goes for the trade.

We don't want to retreat to g2 and get tangled up.

So we'll capture.

rnbqk2r/ppp2p2/3b2p1/8/3P2p1/6P1/PPP1P2P.text:
The h-pawn recaptures, and the rook is open.

Do you see the threat for Black now?

The threat was to capture the g3-pawn!

That's why Qd3 comes to the rescue, covering the g-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/8/8/PPPPP1PP/RN.text:
And now Black offers another pawn.

Their idea is simple: for the price of a pawn, they want to have an already developed dark-squared bishop and an open light-squared bishop.

I say let them have it.

The compensation they get isn't good enough for them.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5.

The idea behind this gambit is to follow it up with either ...d6, trying to develop quickly, or ...Nc6 as we will see in the Sidelines study.

Expect to see 1...e5 only 10% of the time, even though that is almost 5 million games.

We'll take. After all, this isn't a gambit to reject.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 2 of the Bird opening course, we will take a look at a deviation on the very first move!

Abstaining from the more positional 1...d5, some Black players like to gambit against unpopular openings like the Bird.

1...e5 is dangerous, but suboptimal, and can easily lead to great positions for White.

We will open with the Bird.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2nq4/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPPB1PP.text:
And so will we, safe and sound.

With little to no compensation for the pawn, White is simply better.

If Black continues to be aggressive with a move like ...f5, even d4 followed by c4 and Nd2 to trade the bishops is a good idea.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/8/8/5NP1/PPPPP1B.text:
Not much to do for Black but continue natural development.

We've developed the kingside fully...

So it's time to castle.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1b1PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
But we should just develop.

If they capture, they will only trade off an active piece.

White is much better here.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1b1PP3/2N5/PPP3P.text: Black can try to pin our knight...

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/6n1/8/1b1PP3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
Black pins our queenside knight...

But that doesn't bother us.

They can capture if they like. We'll simply develop.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5nn1/8/1b1PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text: The knight comes out to f6, and now there is an actual threat on the e4-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5nn1/8/1b1PP3/2NB1N2/PP.text:
So we protect it.

Everything is safe and sound, and we have gotten what every player wishes out of the opening.

The kingside is developed and we'll castle next.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/8/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
The move 2...Nc6 is played 22% of the time, in more than 600 000 games.

The idea is that Black develops quickly, and the e5-pawn can't be saved either way.

Let's activate our knight to c3.

This either forces Black to capture on e5, or play ...d6 and transpose back into lines we know.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3P4/2N5/PPP1P1PP.text:
Black retreating to c6 doesn't accomplish anything.

We'll simply play e4, after which we've got two pawns in the center and a huge lead in activity.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/6n1/8/3P4/2N5/PPP1P1PP.text:
Black can try to rotate the knight to the kingside, but this shouldn't change our plan.

And it is very simple, which is the beauty of it.

We simply want two pawns in the center.

After that, we'll develop the knight to f3 and the light-squared bishop - easy moves that play themselves.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/8/2N5/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black captures.

Sure, they've regained the pawn, but at what cost?

We now get to expand in the center with tempo.

And guess what, the e-pawn is coming to e4 as well!

r2q1rk1/2p2ppp/p1pb1n2/7b/8/2NPPN1P/PPP3.text:
And the idea of d3 is to support the e-pawn advancing.

If we can put e4 into motion, we will also get Bg5 out pretty quickly and already start to threaten nasty things in the center.

If somehow not, going for b3 and Bb2 is still a sound plan.

A move like Kh1 could be a prophylactic idea to get off the dark diagonal.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/8/3P2b1/5NP1/PPP1.text:
One such idea could definitely be d4, expanding in the center and opening up the bishop.

Next we'll have to choose between c3 and c4, as well as Bg5.

White is better but has to be careful.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/8/6b1/2N1PN2/PPPP.text:
And we'll castle.

We are up a pawn with a solid position, ready to continue expanding.

White is much better.
Black gets their knight out now...

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/8/6b1/5NP1/PPPPP1.text:
If you see the bishop on g4 you don't have to move the e-pawn.

The knight is already defended by the bishop and the rook.

Let's devise a plan on how to continue development.

r2qk1nr/1pp2ppp/p1nb4/1B6/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
Black will only accelerate that process if they attack our bishop now.

We'll take and get rid of the potentially dangerous knight.

r2qk1nr/2p2ppp/p1pb4/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2PP/.text:
Black's pawns are now doubled and isolated.

We'll castle.

Next, our plan is simple: we want to ask the bishop on g4 a question with h3, then develop the queenside and play in the center.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2nb4/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2PP/.text:
5...Nc6 is more committal than 5...Nf6.

The reason is that we have a clear plan for the light-squared bishop now.

We'll develop it to b5 and pin the knight on c6.

We've seen this motif in the previous chapter as well. Our idea is to capture!

r2qk2r/2p2ppp/p1pb1n2/7b/8/4PN1P/PPPP2P1.text:
Black can retreat and keep the pin.

Chasing the bishop here could be too weakening for the king.

So we'll just get the knight out to c3 instead.

You will see our plan soon.

r2qk2r/2p2ppp/p1pb1n2/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2PP.text:
Black continues to develop.

We'll attack the bishop first.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2nq4/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2PP/R.text:
Black activates the knight to c6 now.

The whole point of this line is that they get to castle queenside as quickly as possible.

Also, we don't really want the knight coming to e5.

So we will unpin.

This looks passive, but remember we are up a pawn and Black has done nothing to actually attack our position.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/6b1/2N1PN2/PPPP.text:
Black castles.

The best square for our bishop now is actually Be2, since Bb5 makes no sense.

It does seem cramped, but it's safe.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/3b4/8/6b1/5N2/PPPPP1PP/.text:
One way do try that is ...Bg4.

Developing both bishops already, Black is attacking our knight and posing some questions.

Their idea is to play ...Nf6 or ...Nc6 next.

The move e3 is often a good idea when Black attacks your knight like this.

Although it pins the knight, it protects it with the queen and we remain flexible.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/6b1/4PN2/PPPP2PP.text:
If Black goes for ...Nf6, they remain open with their options so we have to approach the position a little bit more carefully.

I suggest we simply develop with Nc3.

Nothing can go wrong here.

rn2kbnr/ppp2ppp/3q4/8/6b1/5N2/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black might activate the bishop here, as the other one is blocked.

e3 is logical to open up the light-squared bishop and defend the knight with our queen.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/3q4/8/8/8/PPPPP1PP/RNBQ.text:
Black can also recapture with the queen here.

This looks counter intuitive and is played only 3% of the time.

However, we have to be prepared for anything.

For now, simple development with Nf3 will suffice.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/8/5NP1/PPPPP2P/.text:
Black castles.

We'll fianchetto the bishop.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3b4/8/8/8/PPPPP1PP/RNBQ.text:
Black will most likely recapture with the bishop.

And we will continue development, just like in the Main Lines study.

We have already analyzed Black's aggressive 4...g5, aiming for ...g4.

But what if Black decides to play more of a positional game and develop rapidly, trying to claim an advantage that way?

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/8/5N2/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
A move that definitely signifies rapid development is 4...Nf6.

Expect to face this move 20% of the time.

I recommend a fianchetto approach here.

Black has remained flexible with their last move and they can still try to throw a surprise attack.

This way, we ensure to develop the bishop and castle quickly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/8/8/PPPPP1PP/RN.text:
Black plays d6, as before.

Let's take the pawn as we did in the Main Lines study.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black gambits a pawn.

Let's accept.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we will look at the side lines Black can try to throw our way in the 1...e5 Bird.

For example, they can play 2...Nc6 rather than 2...d6 on move 2, or they can recapture with the queen on move 3 if they do play 2...d6.

These alternatives aren't often the best but are still worth exploring.

We'll open with 1.f4.

1r1q1rk1/p4ppp/b1pbpn2/2pp4/2P2P2/1P1PPN.text:
But we can add a defender to c4. We will continue with moves like Qe2 to defend e3 and Ne5. 

A rook lift can also be possible under the right circumstances.
The rook goes to b8 and pins the b-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/1p1ppppp/p1q2n2/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PP.text:
The queen recaptures.

We're going to fianchetto, which further strengthens our control of e5.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p1qp1n2/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/.text: Black pushes ...d6 to fight for control of e5.

We will play Qe2, d3 Nbd2 and e4. 

Our plans are clear: we will use our central pawn and piece play to attack Black. It is tough to suggest a productive plan for Black.

r1b1kb1r/1pqppppp/p1n2n2/1Bp5/5P2/4PN2/P.text:
Once they waste time begging for this trade, we'll accept it.

This trade gives us even more power over the e5-square.

r1b1kb1r/ppqppppp/2n2n2/1Bp5/5P2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black may try avoiding the doubling of the pawns by bringing their queen out. 

It's a clever move that's not often seen.

We'll just castle for now and wait and see if Black will prompt us to take.

r1b2rk1/p3ppbp/2p2np1/q1p5/N2pPP2/1P1P1N.text:
But Black is in some trouble because they mismanaged their pawn play. 

Our very straightforward plans can get you to a position as favorable as this, because Black often plays planlessly.

Ba3 and Ne5 are two powerful moves that you will be able to play.

r1bq1rk1/p2pppbp/2p2np1/2p5/4PP2/3P1N2/P.text:
They castle. If 8.e5 they play 8...Nd5, so we don't want that.

Instead we'll just castle.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1pp1pn2/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
This is one of the only ways to develop the bishop into an active role.

We push d3, again with our slow plan of a potential e4, Nbd2.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2p2np1/2p5/3pPP2/2NP1N2/.text:
Black pushes and attacks us. 

This is a common reaction, to advance the pawn.

The good thing is that now the block of pawns is frozen and we can start building some pressure against them.

We'll start with Na4.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2p2np1/2pp4/5P2/2NPPN2/P.text:
Black castles.

We'll put e4 on the board. 

We have some attacking ideas like e5 and Qe1 to get the queen to a more active square like h4.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2pp1np1/2p5/4PP2/2NP1N2/.text:
And we have some great attacking ideas: Be3, Qe1 to h4 and Rb1 to defend b2 if necessary. 

It's hard to suggest plans for Black because 9...d5 10.e5 is bad for them.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2pp1np1/2p5/4PP2/3P1N2/P.text: Black gets ready to develop their light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/2pbpn2/2pp4/2P2P2/1P2PN2/.text:
Black castles.

And we'll castle as well.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2nppn2/8/3P1P2/P1NB1N2/.text:
We develop the queen, and we have a rich game with various options. 

We can play Bd2 intending 0-0-0, followed by a kingside attack. 

Alternatively, we can castle short and place our rooks on e1/f1, then slowly improve with Ne4.

r1bqk1nr/p2pppbp/2p3p1/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPPP.text:
Taking towards the center is the best move. 

There's no reason to take away from the center and leave us with even more central control.

Now d3 serves multiple purposes. 

We can play e4 if needed and we also control some central squares.

r1bqk1nr/p3ppbp/2p3p1/2pp4/5P2/3PPN2/PPP.text:
Black can push in the center right away.

We'll castle. 

They seem to have a strong block of pawns controlling many squares.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/1Bp5/5P2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black fianchettoes. 

Their hope is to have their dark-squared bishop actively pressure us on the diagonal.

We will take on c6.

r1bqk2r/p2pppbp/2p2np1/2p5/5P2/3PPN2/PPP.text:
Black could delay playing in the center like this. 

They may simply want to develop.

We'll play our slow pawn advance with e4.

r1bqk2r/p3ppbp/2p2np1/2pp4/5P2/3PPN2/PPP.text:
They develop their knight to castle kingside.

But we also develop our knight. 

There isn't much we can do about the block of pawns right now, but we are preparing e4.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2pbpn2/2pp4/2P2P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black develops their bishop to d6, fighting for e5.

But after Bb2 we have two pieces and a pawn controlling e5.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2nppn2/8/3P1P2/2NB1N2/PP.text:
The bishop comes out to e7.

We'll take control of the b4-square.

This prevents ...Nb4 attacking our bishop.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/P1.text:
The bishop is developed.

We'll fianchetto, with long range pressure on the diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
Black recapturing towards the center is best because they keep the option alive of playing ...d5.

We should therefore put our c4-pawn up and claim some central control.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/2pp4/2P2P2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black now pushes 6...d5. 

We will leave the pawn tension as it is and focus on development.

With b3, we support c4 and get ready to fianchetto.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/1Bp5/5P2/4PN2/P.text:
This move ignores our intention to take on c6 and seeks to push d5.

We'll take and double the pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
This move is played less than 10% of times, but I still feel it's natural and worth looking at.

It's developing both knights before bishops, after all.

Our bishop to b5 idea works here, too.

Our aim is to damage the pawns and remove one of Black's best pieces that challenges our dark-square complex in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/8/3P1P2/5N2/PPP3.text:
Black develops their other knight. 

This is the most popular move, but it allows our d5 idea.

After d5, we force the black knight to a bad square.

On b4, the knight will be useless because we'll defend d5 right away and the knight will be attacking nothing.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/8/3P1P2/3B1N2/PPP.text:
Black brings out the other knight.

As will we.

We have two powerful central pawns backed up by our pieces.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPPP.text:
Black recaptures away from the center. 

This move is inferior because it gives us e5 to work with. d6 cannot be played anymore.

We'll fianchetto and focus on increasing our control of e5.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPP.text:
About 20% of games go like this. 

This move order stops us playing b3 and Bb2.

We control the b4-square.

This avoids ...Nb4 attacking our bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
This is Black's most popular second move when they start with 1...c5. 

You can expect it close to 50% of times. 

Once the c-pawn is pushed, players like to develop this knight and have it fight for central control.

We will now build our powerful pawn chain and open up our light-squared bishop.

Our ideas for many of these lines will include Bb5 to take on c6 and reduce Black's central grip.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPPP2.text:
The most popular move here, 3...d5, transposes back to Chapter 1, Study 2. This alternative is played in about 22% of games.

Black defends c5 and gets ready to develop their light-squared bishop.

We'll push 4.d4 and create tension in the center.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/3p1P2/4PN2/PPP3P.text:
You'll most likely see this capture because Black wants to avoid us capturing on c5 ourselves.

We'll recapture, with a strong central pawn on d4. 

Our 6.d5 idea is hard to stop. 

In fact, 5...g6 and 5...Bg4 can also be met with 6.d5!

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/8/3P1P2/5N2/PPP3PP.text:
This move prevents us from pushing d5 and attacking the knight on c6. 

There are about 5,000 games like this on the database (16% of the total), so it isn't unreasonable that someone could play it against you.

We will simply develop our light-squared bishop.

r2q1rk1/p4ppp/b1pbpn2/2pp4/2P2P2/1P2PN2/.text:
Black is able to get some pressure against our queenside in this variation.

But it's nothing we won't be able to handle with some clean, logical moves.

d3 supports our c-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pb2bppp/1pp1pn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2.text:
Black is in serious trouble because the doubled c-pawns don't contribute much and rather block the bishops. 

We will play Nbd2 and Qe2 and build on our position from there.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/3P4/2P2P2/2NB1N2.text:
And so do we. 

We have some plans like Kh1 to get our king off the diagonal, and then develop our pieces around our strong center and dominate the game with our spatial advantage.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/3P4/2P2P2/2N2N2/P.text:
Black fianchettoes.

We'll play Bd3, intending to castle next. Our central control is yet to be challenged. 

Like I said, ...e6 at various points accomplishes very little.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/3P4/2P2P2/5N2/PP.text:
This is one of the few options for the dark-squared bishop.

We'll just continue developing with Nc3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/3P4/5P2/5N2/PPP3P.text:
If we force the knight back, we can say we have a good position.

We'll now build our strong center with 7.c4. 

Black will have a tough time challenging it. 7...e6 8.Nc3 and the d5-pawn is still holding up strong.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black controls the d4-square using the flank pawn. 

This move occurs about 11% of the time in more than 5 million games.

Our plan stays consistent. We want to control the central e5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
A very popular move against the Bird Opening is 1...c5. 

Black plays in a Sicilian-fashion. 

We want to understand how this flank move affects our strategy, and for that we will use a Bb5 idea to take their knight on c6 most of the time.

We'll go for The Bird.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2q2np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2P3/PB.text: And that is, when the queen recaptures...

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/2q2np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2PB2/P.text:
Now Bf3 is strong, to improve the bishop and target the center.

Next, a good idea would be d3+Nd2 to finish development and we've got a healthy, although equal, position.

r1b2rk1/ppq1ppbp/2n2np1/2ppN3/5P2/1P2P3/.text:
Black will most likely defend with the queen and prepare to recapture.

The knight on c6 can be a problematic piece, as we know...

So we will get rid of it.

There is another idea behind this trade.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/2P2P2/1P2P.text:
On the other hand, we are the ones that definitely can expand further.

And we will do so with d4!

Trading in the center and opening up the position will benefit us as we have a little more space.

Also, there could be a possibility of trading the knights.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/8/2Pp1P2/1P2PN.text:
Black takes.

It's important to keep in mind that we don't want to recapture with the pawn.

This could keep our bishop blocked in after ...e6, since we would be reluctant to push d5.

We will recapture with the knight instead and keep our bishop active.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p2p1np1/8/2PQ1P2/1P2P3/.text:
Taking with the queen is better.

Now we even have a strong battery on the dark squares and Black has to be a little bit careful.

If Black goes for something like ...Nh5, retreating to d2 is fine since we don't mind trading the bishops.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p2p1np1/8/2Pn1P2/1P2P3/.text: When Black captures, we again prefer to avoid capturing with the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
Finally, once we've committed the bishop, Black goes for ...Nc6.

Definitely tricky.

We'll castle.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/2pp4/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
The active ...d5 is the more popular choice, which you will encounter 44% of the time.

This does take central space but the d5-pawn could be a little bit loose if Black doesn't want to protect it with ...e6 and block the bishop.

As seen before, we should let Black have the e4-square and play on the dark squares, which is why we will jump into the center right away with Ne5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
A solid setup that counters our dark-squared pawn chain is ...d6, seen 35% of the time.

Black simply wants to open up the bishop without worrying about being over-extended in the center.

Also, we can't play Ne5 now.

Since Black has given us extra space, let's use it with c4.

We've got control over both d5 and e5 now and it's not that easy for Black to expand further.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2ppB3/5P2/1P2P3/P1.text:
It's better to recapture with the bishop and keep it active.

Black can't attack it with ...d6.

Next, we've got two viable plans:

We can either play Nc3 and Bf3 to start targeting the d5-pawn, or we can choose d3 and Nd2 with a more solid approach.

Either way, an active kingside idea is Qe1 and Qh4.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pppbp/5np1/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Black castles here.

As already mentioned, we don't have many squares for the light-squared bishop in this setup.

So e2 will suffice.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/2p5/5P2/1P2PN2/P1P.text:
Black develops the bishop.

And so will we, of course.

In this variation, both sides will develop naturally until a breaking point arrives.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2p5/5P2/4PN2/PPPP.text:
And Black abstains from the early ...Nc6 for a reason.

They don't want to run into Bb5 as we've seen in the previous study.

As mentioned, this is the most problematic move-order, since there is now no point to Bb5.

So we have a new plan.

Since we've created a dark-squared pawn chain in the center, we will counter Black's fianchetto with our own.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
And so does Black, thus controlling each of the central squares with a pawn and a knight respectively.

This move is played only 2% of the time in more than 70 000 games.

Since we can't play e4, let's go for e3 and fight on the dark squares.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black goes for ...c5, controlling the d4-square.

We will get the knight out with Nf3...

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The second study of this chapter will focus on Black going with the c5+Nf6 setup.

It's actually the trickiest move order for us, since Black prevents some of our key ideas when they play like this.

We will start with the Bird.

1rbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NP.text:
Black supports the push, but we won't let it happen.

Let's play a4 and completely lock down the queenside.

1rbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p2p1np1/2p5/P1PnPP2/2NP.text:
Black doesn't have many active options now other than centralizing the knight.

We will trade in this instance.

1rbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p2p1np1/8/P1PpPP2/2NP4/.text:
The pawn recaptures...

And we will centralize the knight.

The idea is that we want to trade off Black's important kingside defender and push f5 at some point to attack.

1rbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p2p2p1/3n4/P1PpPP2/3P4/.text:
Black takes.

We'll recapture with the c-pawn.

1rbq1rk1/4ppbp/p2p2p1/1p1P4/P2pPP2/3P4/1.text: Sure, it does allow ...b5 but it keeps our center intact.

1rbq1rk1/4ppbp/p2p2p1/Pp1P4/3pPP2/3P4/1P.text:
We can push rather than opening up Black's rook and block the file with b4 next move.

As mentioned, f5 is coming.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NP.text:
Another plan that Black can go for is the queenside plan with ...a6.

Their main idea is ...Rb8 and ...b5.

Since they let us expand in the center, they want the queenside.

We can use this time to play the prophylactic Kh1 and get the king away from the dangerous dark diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NP1.text:
Black gets the knight out...

And we will castle.

r1br2k1/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/8/2B1PP2/2P1BN2/P.text:
And we will get the bishop to e3 with a clear plan ahead.

That plan is to bring the rooks to the center and expand even further with g4 and h3.

I would say that our position is more comfortable.

r1br2k1/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/8/2B1PP2/2P2N2/PP.text: Black activates the knight to c6...

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NPBb.text:
Black takes.

We will recapture with the bishop.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P1PPb1/2NP1.text:
Black could go for further development here, with the plan of capturing on f3 and playing ...Nd4.

This is the alternative to going for a queenside plan.

We will let them make the trade but prepare for the knight to jump into the center.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NPBQ2.text:
And we will recapture with a now active queen.

We have the momentum and will play f5 soon.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NPBn2.text: This will push Black towards trading on f3 at some point.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2PnPP2/2NPBB2.text:
We don't have to trade again when the knight comes to the center.

Instead, a good plan is Rb1 with the idea of b4 to disrupt Black's structure protecting the knight.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/1p2p3/2p1N1P1/4pP2/1P2P.text:
And now we can centralize our own knight on e5, resembling lines analyzed earlier in this chapter.

From there, it can jump to g4 and control some key dark squares near Black's king.

Our queen can join the attack on h5 and we will get the rest of the pieces out.

White is better.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/1p2p3/2pp2P1/4nP2/1P1BP.text:
But ...c5 looks much more active.

It is a mistake, though.

Because it allows this trade from us, with an easy plan to attack afterwards.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p2p3/3p4/4nPP1/1P1BPN.text:
Especially if the knight jumps to e4.

We don't want Black to infiltrate with a move like ...Bh4.

So we will play g5 and block the bishop.

Now Black should probably continue with a solid move like ...Nd7.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p2pn2/3p4/5P2/1P1BPN2.text:
Black has to play actively, so they try to counter with ...d5.

It does grab space, but blocks the bishop and doesn't do anything about our plans.

Black probably wants to centralize the knight.

We will push!

g5 is coming.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1ppnp/1p1p2p1/6P1/5P2/1P2PN2.text:
A normal developing move is 9...d6. 

Black wants to get the knight out and also prepare a potential expansion like ...e5.

We have a fantastic plan of h4, h5 to open up the h-file. 

We will of course first play Nc3 and 0-0-0 so that our pieces can help us in our attack of the kingside.

rn1q1rk1/pbppbppp/1p2pn2/8/5P2/1P1BPN2/P.text:
And once Black castles...

Let Rg1 come as a sort of a surprise.

We want to push the g-pawn next and attack.

You will notice that our king will actually be safe in the center.

rn1q1rk1/pbppppbp/1p3np1/8/5PP1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black castles. 

They can now take on g4 because the bishop is defended.

But we'll push! 

And just like that we have a space advantage on the kingside, and we will trade one of Black's important king defenders.

rn1q1rk1/pbppppbp/1p4p1/6Pn/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
The knight goes to h5.

We'll trade.

rn1q1rk1/pbppppnp/1p4p1/6P1/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
They recapture.

And we'll fianchetto our light-squared bishop. 

We aren't allowing Black to keep complete control of any diagonal.

rn1qk2r/pbppbppp/1p2pn2/8/5P2/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Now Black is ready to castle.

Keep in mind that it is possible for you to play Rg1 even here, but Black has not castled yet.

And an early Rg1 might give them second thoughts about doing so.

So I suggest we just develop with Bd3.

rn1qk2r/pbppppbp/1p3np1/8/5P2/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
And Black will fianchetto. 

We now have a chance of doing something interesting.

With 5...Bg7, Black got themselves in a pin. 

They cannot take on g4 so we push it!

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2pn2/8/5P2/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black opens up their bishop...

And we will do the same with ours, connecting the pawn chain.

rn1qkb1r/pbpppp1p/1p3np1/8/5P2/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black wants to fianchetto on g7 as well. 

This is a dynamic and fun line. 

With the double fianchetto, Black hopes to exert pressure along both diagonals.

We will play our normal move to support our forward f4-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pbpppppp/1p3n2/8/5P2/1P3N2/P1PP.text:
They choose to fianchetto now...

And so will we.

It is almost a symmetrical position, with the exception that we have a pawn on f4 that covers e5 as well.

When Black opts for this line, it is important to know our plan from the start.

It is to develop the bishops, play Rg1 at some point and attack the king.

rnb2rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/4PP2/2P2N2/PP4PP/.text:
Sure, Black can castle and we can't.

But we have a lot more central space and a lead in activity.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/2N2N2.text:
And if Black goes for this push...

Even d3 is completely sufficient, opening up the bishop.

We will most likely castle next.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1pp1p/4n1p1/3P4/4P3/2b1BN2/P.text:
The only way to save it is this trade.

We will recapture.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2P1PP2/2N2N2/.text:
It is logical for Black to stop e5 with ...d6.

Their main ideas will revolve around ...c5 to prevent d4 and fight back in the center.

We will activate the bishop in the meantime.

We don't have to hurry with a move like d4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/4n1p1/8/3PP3/2N1BN2/PP.text:
Once Black castles, now it is okay to push d5, as there is no ...Nc5.

So we will play it!

If you take a look at the position, Black actually doesn't have a free square for the knight.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/7n/3PP3/2N2N2/PP2B.text:
And so will we.

The bishop is coming out next and the knight is still weak, stuck on the edge of the board.

Our compensation lies in activity and the big center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppnp/6p1/3P4/4P3/2P1BN2/P5P.text:
And now the knight gets the square on g7.

But trading off the strong dark-squared bishop like this and leaving us with a bishop pair is probably not optimal for Black.

We will continue naturally, getting the queen out.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pnp/4p1p1/3P4/2B1P3/2P1BN2/.text:
But we can develop and defend.

Castling is next.

As mentioned, we have more central space, a lead in activity and the bishop pair: good compensation for the pawn.

The position is still equal if Black plays correctly, however.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pnp/4p1p1/3P4/4P3/2P1BN2/P2.text: Black can try to undermine our structure if they like.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P2P2/2N2N2/PP1.text:
A less confrontational move here is castling instead of ...d5.

Black wants to give us complete control of the center and undermine our structure at some point.

Since the knight is now controlling the e4-square, let's play e4!

We are building a huge center.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/4n1p1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PP4P.text:
Black will most likely retreat to e6.

The d4-pawn is under attack, and we don't want to push d5 and allow ...Nc5 with further pressure.

So we will simply protect the pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/2P2P2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Although this central move does not lose the game immediately, it leads to tricky positions and might give us a slight advantage in the long run.

We will take on d5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3n4/5P2/2N2N2/PP1PP.text:
The knight recaptures and attacks f4.

But it has left the f6-square, which means that no piece is controlling e4 now.

So we will play it!

Note that the f4-pawn is hanging.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/7n/3PP3/2N2N2/PP4PP.text:
Going to h5 is passive.

We will just get the bishop out.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/4PP2/2n2N2/PP1P2P.text:
They can capture the knight here.

If we recapture with the b-pawn with hopes of playing d4, Black actually has ...c5.

So I recommend recapturing with the d-pawn.

This keeps the bishop on g7 restricted and offers a trade of queens.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/4Pn2/2N2N2/PP1P2P.text:
Taking the pawn is not a blunder, but gives us a lot of space and a comfortable position.

We now get to place both pawns in the center with tempo.

Black's knight is under attack.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P2P2/5N2/PP1PP1.text:
Black goes ahead with their plan...

And so will we.

Since Black has allowed it, we have strong control over both central squares.

rnbqkb1r/p1pppppp/1p3n2/8/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1.text:
The move 2...b6 is only played 3% of the time, but signifies a specific setup for Black that turns out not to be that bad at all. 

Black wants to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and claim an even bigger clamp on e4.

We will do the same with our bishop.

If Black wants the e4-square, we will get the e5-square.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1P.text:
The most common move for Black in this position is 2...g6, occurring almost 30% of the time.

Already controlling the center, Black wants to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

We have already covered 2...e6 within ...d5-e6-Nf6.

Since we cannot play e4, I recommend we take control of the d5 in another way, which is c4.

The idea is to activate both knights behind the respective pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
Black chooses to develop the knight first.

This is another way of controlling the center and preventing our e-pawn from advancing to e4.

It is played 6% of the time, which is still more than 3 million games in the database.

We'll develop the knight behind the pawn.

Black will not be playing ...e5 any time soon.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The first study of Chapter 4 will deal with Black's ...Nf6 setups on move 1.

Black doesn't always have to respond with 1...d5 or 1...c5, and there are many options on move 1 which lead to different kinds of positions.

Let's see how to play against this move, starting with our opening move of 1.f4.

rnbr2k1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2B1PP2/2P2N2/PP4P.text:
Black improves the rook with tempo, but we have a great square for the king to hide on.

And that's c2.

The king is completely safe and we can continue development.

r2q1rk1/pppnnpbp/3p2p1/4p3/3PPP2/2P1BQ1P.text:
And so do we.

We castled long because we want to use our central and kingside space to expand and attack further.

This is the easiest with moves like g4 and h4.

We have got some advantage already.
Black gets the king to safety...

r2qk1nr/pppn1pbp/3p2p1/4p3/3PPP2/2P2Q1P/.text:
Once ...e5 arrives, no panic.

Capturing on e5 only opens up the position for Black.

Our center is already powerful and we should keep it as such.

So we will protect the center calmly with Be3.

r2qk1nr/pppnppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPP2/2P2b1P/PP.text:
So they capture.

We will take back with the queen, of course.

r2qk1nr/pppnppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPPb1/2P2N2/PP.text:
They opt to develop instead...

And we will attack the bishop on g4.

Since the knight on d7 is blocking the bishop from retreating all the way, Black doesn't have many options here.

r2qk2r/pppnnpbp/3p2p1/4p3/3PPP2/2P1BQ1P/.text:
Black activates the other knight.

Although they are going to castle next move, their pieces aren't exactly active.

Meanwhile we will look to castle long.

rn1qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPPb1/5N2/PPP.text:
Instead of activating the knight, Black can choose to get the bishop out and pin our knight on f3.

This could be useful if we are not careful, as Black wants to capture on f3 while attacking d4.

So we will defend the center.

They can capture on f3 now all they want.

rnbq1rk1/pp2npbp/4p1p1/2ppP3/3P1P2/2PB1N.text:
We need the c3-square to defend the center and create this beautiful and strong pawn structure.

White is already slightly better.

We'll get the bishop out to e3 and could even have plans of pushing g4 at some point.

rnbq1rk1/pp2npbp/4p1p1/2ppP3/3P1P2/3B1N2.text: And if Black continues undermining our structure, we abstained from playing Nc3 for a reason.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1npbp/4p1p1/3p4/3PPP2/3B1N2/.text:
Expect to see ...d5 at some point.

Black's ...e6 move supports it after all.

We don't want to capture and open up the position in Black's favor.

It's better to open up our bishop while grabbing space with e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/4P3/2PP4/2N2N1P/.text:
And we will get the second knight out.

We did push a lot of pawns in the opening, but Black didn't have any concrete counterplay and we will manage to consolidate very soon.

Namely with moves like Be3, Be2 and O-O.

White is better.

rnbq1rk1/ppppnpbp/4p1p1/8/3PPP2/3B1N2/PP.text:
Black castles.

And so do we.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/4PP2/5N2/PPPP2.text:
The most common move after 3.e4 is ...d6, played 37% of the time.

Black wants to play King's Indian style.

That means activating the kingside quickly and fighting back with ...e5 or ...c5.

Since Black has allowed it, let's take the center!

We've got three strong pawns controlling it.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/4p1p1/8/4PP2/5N2/PPPP2.text:
3...e6 is played 23% of the time, and comes with the clear intention of supporting the ...d5 push.

However, Black gives us the center completely after d4.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1PP.text:
And if they fianchetto...

That is exactly what we will play.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/4P3/2PP4/5N2/PP4P.text:
Black escapes to b6.

Our knight on f3 is our only developed piece and holds our position together.

We must not allow ...Bg4 to pin it.

So we will play h3.

Now our important defender can't be attacked easily.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/3PPP2/5N2/PPP3.text:
When Black activates the knight and attacks the e4-pawn, we don't have to protect it.

We can push it right away!

This is one of the benefits of having a pawn on f4 early.

It might seem like it is dangerous to push this far this early, but Black is the one who will have to move a piece more times in the opening.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/4p3/3P1P2/5N2/PPP3.text:
If Black takes...

We will recapture with the f-pawn.

This avoids the queen trade and opens up our bishop.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PPP3PP.text:
If Black places the knight in the center, don't be afraid to attack it again.

This is not overextending as we are building a big center and will reinforce it with a lot of pieces to come.

rnbqk2r/ppppnpbp/4p1p1/8/3PPP2/5N2/PPP3P.text:
On the other hand, they want to stay solid and castle, while aiming to strike back with both ...d5 and ...c5 at some point.

We will continue in a natural manner, developing our bishop and preparing to castle ourselves.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/R.text:
And Black goes for the immediate ...g6.

These kinds of setups can be played against basically any opening, but Black does cede the center.

It is played 5% of the time, amounting to more than 2.3 million games.

We will get the knight out. Our main idea is to go for e4 since Black has allowed it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In the second study, we will analyze positions after 1...g6.

The main difference between these positions and the positions after 1...Nf6 and 2...g6 is that Black doesn't control the e4-square when they fianchetto.

That means that we can get an early e4 in.

We will open with the Bird.
